e-8294.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Cartesian Function With Respect to Plane Polar Coordinates
e-8294.problem: Given that $f(x,y)=\dfrac12x^2+y^2,$ find $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial \theta},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta)$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
e-8294.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta,$ where $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =-(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

e-8295.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Polar Function With Respect to Cartesian Coordinates
e-8295.problem: Given that $w(r, \theta)=r \cos 3\theta,$ find $\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta)$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
e-8295.worked_solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial r}\cos\theta - \dfrac{1}{r}\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial \theta}\sin\theta
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r}=\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta ,\,\frac{∂w}{∂\theta }=-3r\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x} & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}(-3r\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta +3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem: Given that $f(x,y)={x}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
after.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +0\,(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =2r{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: Given that $h(x,y)={x}^{2}y,$ find $\frac{∂h}{∂r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
after.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $h(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r} & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂h}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂g}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x}=2xy,\,\frac{∂h}{∂y}={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =2{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & ={r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r} & =(2{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =3{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: Given that $g(x,y)={y}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂g}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
after.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $g(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂g}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂g}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂g}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $g$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x}=0,\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =0, \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂\theta } & =0\,(-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )+(2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem: Given that $w(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}),$ find $\frac{∂w}{∂r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
after.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $w(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r} & =\frac{∂w}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂w}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂w}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂w}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x}=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},\,\frac{∂w}{∂y}=\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x} & =\frac{2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }, \\ \frac{∂w}{∂y} & =\frac{2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r} & =(\frac{2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta })\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +(\frac{2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta })\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{2r({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{2}{r}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem: Given that $w(r,\theta )=r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ,$ find $\frac{∂w}{∂y},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
after.worked_solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂w}{∂y}=\frac{∂w}{∂r}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂w}{∂\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r}=\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ,\,\frac{∂w}{∂\theta }=-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}(-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Given that w(r,θ)=rcos⁡2θ, find ∂w∂y, where (x,y) are Cartesian coordinates and (r,θ) are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

a
cos⁡2θ(sin⁡θ−2cos⁡θ)
b
cos⁡2θsin⁡θ−2cos⁡θsin⁡2θ
c
sin⁡θ+2cos⁡θ
d
sin⁡2θ(sin⁡θ−2cos⁡θ)
e
−2sin⁡2θcos⁡θ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

∂w∂y=∂w∂rsin⁡θ+1r∂w∂θcos⁡θ.

First, we find the partial derivatives of w with respect to r and θ:

∂w∂r=cos⁡2θ,∂w∂θ=−2rsin⁡2θ

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

∂w∂y=(cos⁡2θ)sin⁡θ+1r(−2rsin⁡2θ)cos⁡θ=cos⁡2θsin⁡θ−2cos⁡θsin⁡2θ.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Polar Function With Respect to Cartesian Coordinates
content.problem: Given that $w(r,\theta )=r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ,$ find $\frac{∂w}{∂y},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
content.worked_solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂w}{∂y}=\frac{∂w}{∂r}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂w}{∂\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r}=\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ,\,\frac{∂w}{∂\theta }=-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}(-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem: Given that $f(r,\theta )=r\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ,$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
after.worked_solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{∂f}{∂r}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r}=\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ,\,\frac{∂f}{∂\theta }=2r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +2{sin}^{3}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{sin}^{3}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Polar Function With Respect to Cartesian Coordinates
content.problem: Given that $f(r,\theta )=r\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ,$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
content.worked_solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{∂f}{∂r}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r}=\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ,\,\frac{∂f}{∂\theta }=2r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +2{sin}^{3}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{sin}^{3}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$
